rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 3.1-3.2, Tables 1-2, Figs. 9-13 - the paper reports its own field data: advised net irrigation depths over three or more seasons in three pilot areas, farmer adherence estimates for 17 pilot areas (499 collaborating farmers, ~100,000 ha), and results of 875 field evaluations of drip, solid-set sprinkler and center-pivot systems (uniformity and working pressure distributions).
rows.notes: The study is a descriptive account of the SIAR irrigation advisory service, with its own field evaluation and adherence data. It does not test or report any result on on-demand irrigation networks, nor does it measure water-use inefficiency arising from inadequate scheduling under such networks. The closest statements are normative (the distribution network must deliver required flows timely for any delivery scheme) or observational on adherence to advice (lower in Tajo-basin areas where water is paid by surface, with 'type of distribution network' listed among factors affecting follow-up, without data). No own evidence on the claimed harm of on-demand networks; the technology studied (advisory service, on-farm system evaluation) differs from the one in the passage.

notes: Full text appears complete. The paper mixes description of the service's methodology (FAO water balance, MOPECO model) with its own operational results; the MOPECO gross-margin/depth curves are model outputs not compared with measured yields here.
